nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: A client books a basic polish manicure with no enhancements. After washing and sanitizing the hands, what is the remaining sequence?

options.a: Polish first so color can dry while you shape and push
options.b: Oil the nails, apply polish, then file the free edge
options.c: Shape, do allowed cuticle work, nourish, then polish last
options.d: Nip living eponychium, polish, then sanitize the hands last

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: After sanitizing, shape the free edge on a dry-enough nail, then perform only licensed cuticle work, apply oil or lotion, and polish last so oil does not sit under color. Polish first traps debris and makes shaping messy. Live-skin nipping is outside typical nail-tech cuticle work.

distractorExplanations.a: Polish belongs last; painting first blocks clean filing and allowed cuticle work.
distractorExplanations.b: Oil under lacquer causes peeling, and filing after color chips the free edge.
distractorExplanations.d: The eponychium is living tissue; nipping it is not licensed cuticle removal, and sanitizing belongs at the start.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: You soak fingers before using a nipper near the nail fold. What is that soak actually for?

options.a: Softening living eponychium so it can be trimmed flush
options.b: Disinfecting the fold so implements no longer need EPA soak
options.c: Hardening leftover cuticle so it clips as one strip
options.d: Softening nonliving cuticle you are licensed to remove

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: A water soak only hydrates and loosens dead cuticle on the plate. The eponychium is living skin at the proximal fold; soaking does not make it legal or safe to cut. The soak is also not a disinfectant step for tools or tissue.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses cuticle (dead tissue on the plate) with eponychium (living skin you do not trim).
distractorExplanations.b: Warm water is not disinfection; metal implements still need proper EPA disinfection.
distractorExplanations.c: Soaking softens tissue; it does not harden cuticle for a cleaner clip.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: A soak-off gel polish bottle specifies thin coats and a listed LED time. How should you apply and cure?

options.a: Thin coats cured in the lamp and time the product names
options.b: One thick coat cured longer so a second layer is skipped
options.c: Thin coats left to air-dry the way lacquer does
options.d: Any salon UV or LED lamp run for a flat two minutes

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: Gel polish polymerizes only under the wavelength and time the photoinitiators need, in thin layers so light reaches the bottom. Thick coats wrinkle and undercure. Air-drying is for solvent lacquers. A random lamp or generic two-minute cycle can leave inhibition and allergy risk.

distractorExplanations.b: Extra cure time does not fix a thick coat; the underside still undercures.
distractorExplanations.c: Gel needs a matching lamp; it does not set by solvent evaporation like lacquer.
distractorExplanations.d: Lamp type and seconds are product-specific; a mismatched unit undercures gel.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: A client wants gel polish off without thinning the natural plate. Which removal method is correct?

options.a: Pry lifted gel off with a metal pusher as soon as it peels
options.b: Lightly break the seal, then follow the product soak-off method
options.c: Grind all gel away with a coarse grit until the plate looks chalky
options.d: Soak the nails in warm water until the gel slides off

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: Soak-off gels are designed for acetone (or the maker’s solvent) after a light surface break, not for peeling or coarse grinding. Prying rips keratin layers. Coarse e-file work on the full coating thins the plate. Water does not dissolve cured gel.

distractorExplanations.a: Peeling gel shears layers of the natural plate even if the film has started to lift.
distractorExplanations.c: Coarse full-plate grinding is product-removal abuse; it leaves the keratin thin and chalky.
distractorExplanations.d: Warm water softens skin, not cured gel polymer; soak-off chemistry is solvent-based.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: An acrylic overlay has two weeks of growth, leaving a bare band at the proximal fold. What service addresses that band?

options.a: Spot-glue a stress-area crack and skip any rebalance
options.b: Soak off the entire overlay and rebuild a new set each visit
options.c: Fill and rebalance product in the cuticle-area regrowth
options.d: Add a tip on the free edge to restore lost length

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: A fill (rebalance) replaces product in the new-growth zone near the cuticle and reshapes the apex as the nail grows. Full soak-off is a new set, not routine maintenance. Glue repairs cracks; tips add free-edge length. Neither substitutes for a proximal fill.

distractorExplanations.a: Crack repair is a separate patch; it does not fill the proximal regrowth gap.
distractorExplanations.b: Complete removal every visit is a replacement set, not a maintenance fill.
distractorExplanations.d: A tip lengthens the free edge; the problem described is proximal growth, not length.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: After filing and dehydrating the natural plate, why is primer or bonder applied before acrylic?

options.a: To strip leftover oil and moisture the dehydrator missed
options.b: To seal the finished overlay against later water exposure
options.c: To thin the monomer so the bead stays wet longer
options.d: To promote adhesion of product on the prepared plate

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: Primer or bonder is an adhesion promoter used on a plate that is already filed and dehydrated. Dehydrator removes oil and water. Top coat or sealer gel finishes the surface. Liquid-to-powder ratio, not primer, controls bead wetness.

distractorExplanations.a: Oil and moisture removal is the dehydrator’s job, done before primer.
distractorExplanations.b: Sealing a finished enhancement is top coat or sealer, not plate primer.
distractorExplanations.c: Primer sits on the plate; it is not mixed into monomer to change bead wetness.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: You are shortening and shaping a natural fingernail with a hand file after a soak. Which grit belongs on that plate?

options.a: About 180–240 grit with light, one-direction strokes
options.b: An 80-grit coarse board to drop length in a few passes
options.c: A metal rasp intended for thick plantar callus work
options.d: The coarsest board on the table so the soak can be skipped

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: Natural nails are shaped with a finer grit, commonly about 180–240, using light strokes in one direction to limit peeling. Eighty-grit and metal rasps are for product or callus, not keratin plate. Coarse filing does not replace a soak and will chew the free edge.

distractorExplanations.b: 80-grit is a product/artificial grit; on a natural plate it peels and thins keratin.
distractorExplanations.c: A callus rasp belongs on thick foot skin, not on a fingernail plate.
distractorExplanations.d: Grit does not replace softening; coarsest boards still damage a wet natural edge.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: A client wants a classic French manicure. In that polish design, what is the smile line?

options.a: The pale lunula half-moon sitting over the matrix
options.b: The painted curve of color on the free edge
options.c: A cloudy white band that means product has lifted
options.d: A transverse ridge left by aggressive e-file rings

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: The smile line is the cosmetic curve where the French free-edge color meets the pink or nude bed color. The lunula is anatomy at the base. Lifting looks like a cloudy gap, and e-file rings are grooves in the plate, not a painted design.

distractorExplanations.a: The lunula is the visible matrix half-moon at the base, not the French free-edge curve.
distractorExplanations.c: A white cloudy band is a lift or moisture pocket, not the intended French smile.
distractorExplanations.d: E-file heat rings are damage; they are not the polish line of a French manicure.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: During a pedicure massage the client reports varicose veins on the calf and a healing blister on the heel. What should you avoid?

options.a: Light effleurage on intact skin of the dorsum of the foot
options.b: Any lotion contact anywhere proximal to the ankle bone
options.c: Deep work, broken skin, and flagged varicose-vein areas
options.d: Checking with the client whether pressure still feels comfortable

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: Pedicure massage is comfort-level only. Skip broken skin, deep or medical-style work, and areas the client identifies for varicosities. Light effleurage on intact foot skin is ordinary. Lower-leg work is not banned solely for being above the ankle, and pressure checks are good practice.

distractorExplanations.a: Light stroking on intact skin is standard pedicure comfort massage, not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.b: Massage often includes the lower leg; the issue is veins, open skin, and depth, not the ankle landmark.
distractorExplanations.d: Asking about pressure is a safety check, not something to skip.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: At the end of a basic pedicure you trim toenails with the goal of fewer ingrowns. How should they be cut?

options.a: Round the corners deep into the lateral nail grooves
options.b: Cut flush to the hyponychium so no free edge remains
options.c: Cut a V-notch in the center of the free edge
options.d: Cut straight across, leaving the corners visible

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: Toenails are trimmed straight across with the corners left slightly showing so the plate cannot grow into the sulcus. Rounding into the grooves and cutting to the hyponychium both raise ingrown and injury risk. A center V-notch is a folk myth and does not prevent ingrowns.

distractorExplanations.a: Digging corners into the grooves is a classic setup for ingrown toenails.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing the free edge to the hyponychium exposes the distal fold and invites injury.
distractorExplanations.c: A V-notch does not redirect growth; straight-across trimming is the prevention method.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: A client wants toenails cut “as short as the nail bed,” with no free edge left. What should she hear?

options.a: Cutting into the groove risks injury and infection
options.b: Extra-short nails prevent ingrowns, so the request is safe
options.c: Filing down to the bed is fine if nippers stay in the drawer
options.d: A long soak makes cutting into the groove acceptable

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: A short, visible free edge protects the hyponychium. Cutting or filing into the groove or flush with the bed can injure skin, open a path for infection, and let the corner grow into the sulcus. Soaking only softens keratin; it does not make that cut safe.

distractorExplanations.b: Too-short corners actually increase ingrown risk as they grow into the fold.
distractorExplanations.c: A file to the bed still removes the protective edge; the tool type does not make it safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Hydration does not protect the distal fold from a cut taken into the groove.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: A sidewall pocket of lifted acrylic has moisture underneath. What is the correct next step?

options.a: Run extra adhesive under the lifted edge to reseal it
options.b: Remove the lift and rebalance so water cannot pool
options.c: Paint a thick top coat over the lift to hold the overlay down
options.d: Work cuticle oil into the gap to feed the natural plate

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: A lift is a reservoir for water and microbes (including Pseudomonas “greenies”). The lifted film must come off and the area be rebalanced. Glue, top coat, or oil traps moisture instead of eliminating the pocket.

distractorExplanations.a: Adhesive under a lift seals in moisture and organisms; it is not a repair.
distractorExplanations.c: Top coat over a gap does not reattach product and can lock water in.
distractorExplanations.d: Oil in a lift does not nourish the plate; it adds more debris to a wet pocket.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: Liquid-and-powder acrylic is open at the table. How should monomer be handled during the service?

options.a: Warm the dappen dish so the bead sets faster
options.b: Pour leftover liquid back into the original bottle
options.c: Use ventilation and keep the monomer lid managed
options.d: Dump unused monomer down the salon sink at close

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: EMA monomer vapors need ventilation, and the dish or bottle should stay covered when not dipping to limit fumes and contamination. Heating increases flammable vapor. Used liquid is contaminated and is not returned to stock or poured to a drain; SDS and local rules govern disposal.

distractorExplanations.a: Heat raises flammable vapor and speeds an uncontrolled set; monomer is used at room temperature.
distractorExplanations.b: Powder and debris in used liquid spoil the stock bottle if it is poured back.
distractorExplanations.d: Monomer is not wastewater; leftovers are absorbed and sealed per the SDS, not rinsed to a drain.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: After a nail-art design, how should the detail brush be treated before the next client?

options.a: Pass the still-loaded color brush straight to the next client
options.b: Dip it in monomer and count that as disinfection
options.c: Park it wet in acetone overnight between clients
options.d: Clean product from bristles; monomer is not a disinfectant

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: Art brushes must be cleaned of color or acrylic between clients. Monomer or acetone may dissolve product but are not EPA-registered disinfectants, and acetone wrecks many bristles. A loaded brush is a cross-contamination tool, not a sanitizer.

distractorExplanations.a: A shared, loaded brush transfers product and microbes from nail to nail.
distractorExplanations.b: Monomer is a solvent for acrylic, not an EPA disinfectant for implements.
distractorExplanations.c: Overnight acetone storage damages bristles and still is not disinfection.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.prompt: A first-trimester client asks whether gel polish and acrylic fumes are “doctor-approved.” What is in a nail tech’s scope?

options.a: Promise her that every chemical used at the table is pregnancy-safe
options.b: Follow labels, ventilate, and refer questions to her clinician
options.c: Refuse every nail service until after she delivers
options.d: Recommend a prenatal vitamin that “protects nails”

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-se.explanation: Nail technicians stay in cosmetic scope: follow manufacturer labels, use ventilation, and decline medical claims. Pregnancy is not an automatic salon ban, but safety guarantees and supplement advice are medical practice. Her clinician answers exposure questions.

distractorExplanations.a: A blanket chemical-safety promise is medical advice, not a product-label statement.
distractorExplanations.c: Pregnancy is not a universal contraindication; services proceed per labels and client comfort.
distractorExplanations.d: Suggesting prenatal supplements is outside nail-tech scope.
